GUEST writes the Exploring Race column for the Chicago Tribune. We've spoken with her several times over the past year. So, today we can introduce her as one of our regulars on Talk of the Nation. And this year, with the historic inauguration of Barack Obama, it was a question that we really - I think we gave little more weight to. And - but I do think - and I've heard from many readers who have said that African-American history should be merged with American history, because it cheapens one or both to segregate one from the other. And they forget or don't realize that King also vehemently opposed the Vietnam War for moral reasons, but thought that money and other - that money and other money should be redirected or redistributed to deal with black poverty. HOST: Some people would argue we're - Americans are not particularly well-versed in history, period…
GUEST: Absolutely (Laughing).

And this whole idea that blacks need something separate in order to continue to go forward is very jarring to a lot of readers. HOST: GUEST?
GUEST: Yes. And I absolutely agree. GUEST: Well, and we also have - March is Women's History Month, right? So, I mean, there's (Laughing) - you're right. I mean, we - you can go on and on and on. GUEST: Yeah.

GUEST: It is a very positive way. And I remember there was a study a few years ago that showed that Americans were woefully behind when it came to history. And I think that there should be a push for all of it. But I do believe that there is still some validity in separating and every now and then kind of highlighting or illuminating some parts of - whether it's black history or Hispanic heritage month or Asian-American history.

HOST: And by the way, we've been told by our reference librarian, Kee Malesky, Native American month is November.
GUEST: Ah, OK. That's good to know.

HOST: What do you think, GUEST?

This is what we're taught in school and it's - and the reason why black history came to the fore years ago is because there was this fear that - from Carter G. Woodson - that we wouldn't - that all of the accomplishments would be missed of black Americans. And so, I understand that, and I hear it a lot, that if we didn't talk about it, then maybe it would go away. But I'm not certain that we're that - that we've moved that far ahead, as a country, when it comes to race.

GUEST: Oh, it's my pleasure. Thank you.

I don't think Greenspan could have done much more than the 50 basis points he did. If it had been 75, I don't think the market would have rallied that much more for you -- then 25, we certainly would have sank. I think my sense now is we've got to see the economic data begin to convince us that the recovery has begun, and until that happens it's very hard to make a case for another big move up in equity prices.

HOST: We're going to get an APM. We're going to also get a jobs report this week. These are important numbers -- in fact, it was the NAPM report that many think is what prompted the Fed to cut between meetings last time around. If we still get a lot of weakness, could we see an inter-meeting move? The Fed doesn't have a meeting until late March.
GUEST: You know, it's funny -- I -- well, you're right about a couple of things. One is the NAPM is key, because Greenspan always looks at NAPM, and more importantly now, it's the first piece of reliable data we will get for the month of January. See, the third quarter -- well, actually, the most important numbers were the December numbers, and a lot of them are estimated, simply because of the way, the mechanics, of how they calculate it work -- so the NAPM report becomes that much more important. I don't think, however, that Greenspan will do an inter-meeting cut, because if he does that, politically, I think it will be viewed as he looking at stock prices, which is what he's been accused and said he's not doing. So my feeling would be is we've got 100-basis point cuts now. He's going to give it a chance to work through the economy, and he'll continue to monitor the data. But the interesting thing about the NAPM report will be how was January, how bad was January. And on the heels of the consumer confidence and business confidence numbers that we got earlier, you know, a couple of days ago, it'll be very important to give us a gauge as to how December and January are shaping up in terms of growth.

HOST: It's expected to be weak.
GUEST: It is. And, honestly, the data is still bad. In other words, business -- consumer confidence was really bad -- and business confidence was bad, and business confidence generally leads consumer confidence.

HOST: Right.
GUEST: It's a long way of saying I think consumer confidence is going to go down a little bit more before it goes up. So the data is going to be bad, but I think Greenspan knows a lot of this has to work itself through the economy. HOST: There still are worries about a recession. You don't think we're headed right down into one? You think it's going to come back?

HOST: All right, Frank, good to see you.
GUEST: Thank you.

[Interview, 2001-02-20, Ahead Of The Curve]
HOST: Good morning.
GUEST: Good morning.

HOST: It was all -- it was awhile ago, Friday, of course, but we did have a five-percent drop in the Nasdaq. What was the message sent out by that decline, and do you think we can rebound from here?
GUEST: Well, I think we can, but certainly, you know, the earnings numbers we got in the telecommunications sector really confirm the greatest fear we all have, and that is we're in a profit recession, and that's basically what we're going through now. So we have this confluence of bad earnings in some of the best industries that we can think, like wireless, for example, coupled with this real slowdown in the economy. The data just gets worse and worse. I don't want to paint a terrible picture, because I think it's going to get better. But the fact is is that those are the things that really concern the market, especially the Nasdaq. So, when you get that kind of information, you get that kind of data -- it's what we talked about a few weeks ago: We're going to get bad news, we're probably going to get bad news for another four or five weeks -- presents a buying opportunity, because I think the good news is that we are getting liquidity. It seems to me, given the pick up in monetary aggregates, that we might be in the trough right now, and that is the time you really want to buy equities, right before the economy starts to pick up.

HOST: All right, what would you look at it?
GUEST: Well, I certainly think wireless, for example, certainly presents a good opportunity for a lot of people. I don't think that it's the end of the world for wireless. There are certain concerns about earning, but companies like WorldCom, companies like Nortel, even Corning, for example, which was down, I guess, nine points on Friday, certainly present opportunities for people who are going to be in that sector for the long run. I don't think it's gone. And if you believe the economy is going to pick up, you have to believe that subscribers will -- subscribership will continue to grow in the United States. It will certainly continue to grow in Europe. And so it presents a really good opportunity for long-term investors.

HOST: How do you feel about the retailers, as we swing out of this trough?
GUEST: You know, I can't win on the retailers. Every time I think I've got the retailers figured out -- retailers have it tough: Whether it's the Internet or whether it's traditional retailers, the fact is is that I see no signs of their ability to get any pricing power back. And so because of that, whether or not the economy is good or not really doesn't matter, because retailers have a tough go even when the economy was roaring. So my sense is retailers are going to have to retool. There will probably be more consolidation, and the old clicks and bricks will probably continue to come together. But overall, it's very hard to make a case for retailing, only because of the changing dynamics of the economy and the influence of the Internet. So I would -- I would stand clear of retailers, only because I certainly haven't had a good call on them -- and I really don't see too much upside growth, you know.

HOST: Even with presumably a tax cut coming and the Fed cutting interest rates -- looks good for consumer spending.
GUEST: Oh, it's going to be great for consumer spending, and I think consumer sentiment might be hitting bottom now: You might get one more bad number. So I think psychologically it's good. But again, when consumer spending was up and the economy was roaring, retailers were still having a tough go of it. You get some specialty places, like, I guess, like the Targets of the world: They seem to be able to do well. But you've really got to be able to pick those companies really, really good. And I certainly can't say I know which are going to come out ahead and which aren't.

HOST: When you look at technology -- we were flipping through the paper earlier: There's a full-page ad by one of the box makers, you know, essentially selling you a computer and a free printer for $699...
GUEST: Right.

HOST: ... as you look at the box makers and the tech group as a whole, are you attracted to them? Are you going to wait for them? Are they going to be the ones that lead us out of this time right now, or do you wait and sort of let them pick up a little bit?
GUEST: I would certainly be buying. I'm a believer that until technology moves up and starts to really take the lead, the whole broader market can't move. So I do believe in technology. But the fact is is this great productivity machine that we've built seems to be having some problems right now. So between the layoffs and between the flat-line capital expenditures that we see -- you know, no one's really spending in technology -- I think it's going to be a rough go for the technology sector, but you have to believe in the long run it will be OK, there will be more capital expenditures, people will go back to work, the productivity machine will come back -- and I think the technology sector will lead again: It's just going to take a little time.

GUEST: Thank you.

Prime Minister Erdogan has wanted to finger the main opposition party, the Republican People's Party, for the demonstrations. That's certainly not the case. But one more thing: I think it would be a mistake to pit this as secularists versus Islamists. I think the demands of people in the streets to the extent that you can characterize them are about this authoritarian or illiberal turn in Turkish politics. Many of them say they just - they want their freedom. They want democracy. They want to have a voice in the political system.

HOST: And is it fair to say that some of them are - let me put this another way. Is he going to use, do you think, this new crisis the same way?

This is someone who has in the past not demonstrated a capacity for contrition. So it certainly is a possibility. The problem right now is, is that the authorities have been unable to defuse the protests, and that's primarily because Erdogan himself has not gone out and made conciliatory words, although deputies of his has. I think that people are waiting for Erdogan to make a move and to hopefully calm the streets, and then Turkey can kind of re-evaluate where their next steps are, where Turks, their next steps are in terms of politics. But there's really no evidence that suggests that Erdogan is willing to do that.

HOST: Twenty years ago, demonstrations this size, we would be waiting for the military to step in and say, wait a minute, things are getting out of control. We're going to have to take charge here.

And then beyond, under the threshold of a coup, the military was influential in a variety of ways in politics and played a very, very powerful role in the politics of the country. Beginning in 2003 and 2004, the Justice and Development Party had begun to bring the military under civilian control, which is overall a good thing. It helps create an environment to the emergence of a more democratic Turkey. And since the revelation of this plot, they have gone after the military through the court system, and there are many retired and currently serving officers serving prison terms as a result. So the military's wings have been more than clipped. They don't have the capacity any longer to get involved in politics. The days when Turkish governments were brought down by the military are over. And those elections have been free and fair. And the expectation is that that is the way - the expectation of Turks, that is the way in which to change governments.

HOST: And this description of this hollow democracy, as you describe it, then brings us to the example, the model of Turkey, which has been held out to the newly emerging governments in Egypt, in Libya and in other places as this is the way toward a Islamic democracy.

And to boot, they were successful economically. And I think that many people in the Arab World see Turkey and understand that it has much to offer them. But the problem is just at the time that - not just the United States, but others were holding out Turkey as a model or inspiration for the Arab World - was when this process of hollowing out Turkey's democratic institutions begin, and that this illiberal drift in the Turkish - in Turkish politics was getting underway, yet people continue to hold out the Turkish model. This is certainly not what people in the Arab World initially rose up against - rose up for. Turkey is certainly better than Egypt or Tunisia or Libya. HOST: And so as you look toward the future of Turkey, what lessons do you think the prime minister ought to derive from these demonstrations which are, as you suggest, the greatest challenge in his political career?

I think over the years the increasing, increasingly better electoral returns, a sort of detachment from the people, which is ironic because he made his political career on being close to the people - if he returns to that pragmatism, to that consensus building, if he understands somehow that in a democracy it is not just majority rules, that the voice and desires of the minority deserve a hearing as well, it will certainly put Turkey on a better path. But again, based on recent events, it's unclear that he is able to do that, which is a concern about the future path for Turkey's politics.

HOST: And in terms of the United States, the prime minister has enjoyed a close relationship with President Obama. GUEST: It goes without saying that Turkey throughout has been a strong partner and a strategic ally of the United States. There is not an issue - an important issue in American foreign policy in that part of the world that Turkey is not involved in or touches on in either direct or indirect ways. And I think that's why the administration has been somewhat reluctant previously to call Erdogan out on, for example, freedom of the press and freedom of expression. HOST: You called it a necessity. Why would you describe it that way?

HOST: I was interested in just the mechanics. The five-year-old was being married to a 10-year-old boy.

HOST: And they were - as you and Cynthia Gorney were waiting their arrival, people are expecting them to arrive in - I think the expression was in high spirits and drunk.

HOST: And, of course, the five-year-old's name and prospects were not published on the wedding invitation.

HOST: Is there one story that you heard from the women at the refugee camp who've been rescued - one story that has really stuck with you about what they endured?

She said, how could I abandon those children again? And what really touched me about this - Bingta is a Muslim. The three children that she brought to safety at that refugee camp are all Christians. Now the Islamic uprising in the Northeast has really polarized Nigerians across the country on religious lines. And here's this young girl. When I said to her, you know, how do you feel about the kids? She says, I love them like they are my own. And she, like, beat her chest with both her fists to show how deep her love is for them.

HOST: And the real question now is what happens to them from here?
GUEST: Well, she's hoping that there are parents alive out there that she'll be able to return the children to.

HOST: GUEST, thank you for talking with us.
GUEST: Thanks, Melissa.
